title: Mini-Whiteboards: A Long-Overdue Rant (and Love Letter)
author: Anna Sutton
summary: Anna Sutton, a deputy head with nearly 16 years of teaching experience, makes an unapologetic case that mini-whiteboards (MWBs) are one of the most powerful and most underused tools in the classroom. She contrasts a lesson without MWBs, where confident-seeming cold-call answers mask widespread misunderstanding that only surfaces once independent practice begins, against a lesson with MWBs, where a ten-second reveal instantly exposes the true split between correct and incorrect answers and lets the teacher reteach before moving on. Sutton catalogues everyday uses beyond hinge questions -- retrieval starters, sentence practice, idea collection, and diagrams -- arguing that MWBs are fundamentally instructional decision-making tools that let teachers adapt, redirect, or extend in real time. She is equally candid about the logistical headaches (dried-up pens, lost lids, noisy transitions) and describes how her school solved them with Stabilo whiteboard pencils and double-sided grid/plain boards. The piece closes with a call to action: pick one lesson, use one MWB moment, and let the evidence of what pupils actually know -- rather than assumptions -- drive the next teaching move.
points: Sutton's central argument is that MWBs solve the feedback-loop problem that cold-calling cannot: a teacher can get 100% visibility into every pupil's thinking within ten seconds, rather than inferring understanding from a handful of volunteered answers.

Her two-scenario comparison (no MWBs vs. MWBs) makes the case concretely -- a lesson that looks successful under cold-calling can still collapse during independent practice, whereas the same lesson with MWBs catches the 40% who don't yet understand before independent work begins.

MWBs are framed as more than hinge-question tools: retrieval starters, sentence-level writing checks, idea collection before discussion, and diagram/drawing checks all use the same 'show me' mechanism to expose thinking across subjects.

Sutton insists training and routines are the unglamorous prerequisite for MWBs working at all -- without explicitly taught routines, whiteboards become 'a chaotic nightmare of dried up pens, lost lids, missing boards and noisy transitions.'

A practical logistics fix (Stabilo whiteboard pencils, double-sided grid/plain boards) is offered as a concrete solution to the pen-and-lid problem that derails many attempts to embed MWBs school-wide.
quotes: After 15 years of teaching, I still can’t wrap my head around one thing: how anyone manages without mini-whiteboards. MWBs are simple, cheap, and incredibly powerful. Yet, despite all the blogs, videos, and training out there, they remain underused.
Why? Because they let you see, instantly, what every single pupil knows -- or doesn't. And in that moment, you can make real, informed decisions about your teaching.

You cold call a pupil -- they get it right. You cold call another -- also right. Your brain says: Brilliant- they've got it! The class begins independent practice. And then... as you circulate... mistake after mistake after mistake.
If pupils aren’t trained, MWBs become a chaotic nightmare of dried up pens, lost lids, missing boards and noisy transitions. We’re still working on this as part of our “agreed consistencies.

Mini-whiteboards remain one of the most powerful, underrated, and essential tools in the classroom -- truly the icing that holds your teaching together. And I genuinely don't know how we teach effectively without them.

With MWB's, you can see misconceptions, partial understandings, and the strategies pupils are using to solve problems. When you work out what's happening underneath the answers, you can shape what comes next in a far more targeted way.
